seatMission: Design current, target and transition architecture.
seatResponsibilities: Design current, target, transition, cloud, application and integration architecture.

criterionDimensions.name: Build, buy, partner, retain, and retire decisions

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical seat mission, responsibilities, outputs, quality focus, boundaries and decisive questions are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I reconstruct current architecture from deployed systems, interfaces, data flows, ownership, and operational evidence.
I distinguish documented architecture from the architecture actually running in production.
I identify technology assets and external dependencies material to the decision.
I map business capabilities and critical journeys to enabling technology components.
I identify obsolete, duplicated, fragile, shadow, unsupported, and ownerless technology.
I quantify reliability, performance, cost, incident, support, and dependency evidence when material.
I surface architectural constraints created by contracts, regulation, skills, residency, and migration state.
I preserve uncertainty when current-state evidence is incomplete.
I distinguish architectural causes from visible symptoms such as cost or latency.
I model current state only to the depth needed for the decision.
I derive architecture requirements from business capability, outcomes, constraints, risk, economics, and change.
I distinguish functional requirements from quality attributes.
I prioritize quality attributes by business consequence.
I define architecture requirements for peak, normal, degraded, recovery, and growth conditions.
I translate legal, privacy, security, continuity, and audit obligations into architecture constraints.
I distinguish hard constraints from preferences that may be challenged.
I define data, integration, identity, observability, support, and lifecycle requirements before selecting platforms.
I define testable architecture fitness criteria.
I concentrate flexibility where requirements are likely to change.
I prevent vendor products from being disguised as requirements.
I design target architecture to satisfy required capabilities without unnecessary structural complexity.
I define clear application, service, data, integration, and ownership boundaries.
I separate architecture principles from implementation details.
I choose modularity boundaries from change, ownership, scale, failure, data, and domain evidence.
I prefer simpler deployment models when they meet required outcomes.
I standardize where reuse creates leverage and allow variation where evidence justifies it.
I design failure isolation and graceful degradation proportionate to business consequence.
I include observability, deployment, rollback, supportability, and ownership in target design.
I define authoritative data and lifecycle decisions as part of architecture.
I document material trade-offs and rejected target-state alternatives.
I design explicit transition states between current and target architecture.
I sequence migration to reduce disruption, dependency risk, and irreversible commitment.
I define coexistence, synchronization, compatibility, cutover, rollback, and decommissioning requirements.
I retire obsolete components so migration does not permanently increase complexity.
I identify identity, network, data, security, integration, and capability prerequisites.
I choose migration patterns from evidence rather than fashion.
I define transition checkpoints that can stop or redirect the roadmap.
I account for temporary duplicate cost and burden during coexistence.
I preserve reversibility when uncertainty and consequence justify optionality.
I update transition architecture from migration evidence.
I select cloud, on-premises, edge, SaaS, or hybrid placement from workload evidence.
I distinguish cloud adoption from cloud-native redesign.
I design governed landing zones, resource boundaries, networking, identity, policy, logging, and ownership.
I use managed services when lifecycle economics and reliability justify them.
I avoid self-hosting when it adds risk without sufficient benefit.
I evaluate region, zone, quota, capacity, and service dependencies for critical workloads.
I include configuration, secrets, deployment, backup, and recovery in platform architecture.
I design guardrails that enable safe team autonomy.
I separate shared platform responsibilities from workload responsibilities.
I connect cloud cost to utilization, architecture, reliability, and business value.
I choose application boundaries from domain, data, ownership, change, and reliability needs.
I choose synchronous or asynchronous interaction from latency and failure characteristics.
I define integration contracts, ownership, versioning, idempotency, observability, retry, and error handling.
I reduce point-to-point integration sprawl without creating unnecessary central bottlenecks.
I expose coupling hidden in shared databases, files, exports, jobs, and undocumented APIs.
I design external integrations for vendor failure, rate limits, contract change, and credential rotation.
I govern API and event lifecycles without freezing useful evolution.
I prevent integration platforms from becoming opaque business-logic monoliths.
I make distributed data-consistency expectations explicit.
I test integration under realistic failure, latency, volume, ordering, duplication, and recovery.
I compare build, buy, SaaS, partner, retain, and retire options against common evidence.
I reserve custom engineering for capabilities where ownership creates justified value.
I evaluate commercial products beyond feature lists.
I include implementation, migration, integration, support, renewal, and switching costs.
I identify vendor concentration, lock-in, contract, service, financial, and geopolitical dependencies.
I distinguish useful platform dependency from disproportionate lock-in.
I define exit and data-portability requirements before costly commitments.
I retire legacy when quantified risk and cost justify replacement.
I retain older technology when it remains secure, supportable, economical, and fit.
I record evidence and criteria behind build-buy-retain decisions.
I select Microsoft capabilities for enterprise fit rather than vendor alignment alone.
I distinguish responsibilities across Entra, Azure, Microsoft 365, Power Platform, Fabric, Dynamics, and GitHub.
I design identity around authoritative sources, least privilege, lifecycle, federation, and workload identities.
I evaluate Azure services for reliability, regional availability, cost, integration, security, and operability.
I integrate Microsoft and non-Microsoft systems through explicit standards and contracts.
I use low-code where governed speed outweighs complexity and lifecycle limitations.
I treat Microsoft reference architectures as inputs to judgment, not substitutes for evidence.
I include licensing, tenant boundaries, service limits, support, and commercial dependency in decisions.
I preserve data and integration boundaries that reduce unnecessary proprietary dependence.
I maintain enough cross-platform competence to reject a Microsoft option when another fits better.
I derive service levels and recovery objectives from business consequence.
I design observability for detection, diagnosis, and recovery.
I validate backup, restore, disaster recovery, dependency failure, and capacity exhaustion.
I design deployment and rollback for acceptable change risk.
I distinguish redundancy from resilience and test shared failure modes.
I include patching, upgrades, certificates, secrets, support versions, and end-of-life in lifecycle design.
I automate operational toil while retaining human control for exceptional conditions.
I assign accountable operational ownership before go-live.
I use incidents and near misses as architecture evidence.
I ensure architecture is supportable with realistic skills, staffing, and vendor support.
I evaluate architecture using total lifecycle economics.
I connect technology cost to useful business and workload cost drivers.
I account for cognitive, support, integration, licensing, and coordination cost created by complexity.
I preserve material architecture decisions with rationale and trade-offs.
I distinguish standards that create leverage from central preferences that create drag.
I govern exceptions with rationale, owner, risk, duration, and review.
I use fitness functions and operational evidence to detect architecture drift.
I preserve optionality where uncertainty is high and its cost is justified.
I retire standards when they no longer serve strategy, risk, economics, or engineering effectiveness.
I treat enterprise architecture as a continuing decision capability, not a static diagram repository.
